title: Introduction: The Passing CI Checker That Opened Nothing - 3 Questions Every Automated CI Check Must Answer
text: I'm Ud Sonowane and this is my week on Mickraftoft. Last episode I said the repository had no tests for its step scripts and that CI ran none of it. This week I found out why the checker was green because it was not opening them. Episode 6 listed 10 things the Edestation had not tested. One of them was that there is no independent test suite and CI runs none of it. That was true and I had not asked the obvious followup. The repository does have a conformance checker and it was passing. So what was it checking? Three questions for any automated check that is passing. One, what did it actually open? Count the files by type, not by trust. Two, why is each exclusion there? Is it excluded for

What it is called or for where it lives? Three, how would you know if it stopped working? Break it on purpose and see whether it says so. The ask was to make the checker read the code it claims to check without making it so slow that nobody runs it. Question one. The old run opened 187 files. The new one opens 743. The difference is 476 Python files. The executable surface of 99 recipes. Every step script the pipeline runs was outside the checked set, which means two pull requests past continuous integration without anything compiling a line of their code. The fix is not deleting the entries. Three of those names were fine. The problem is that a base name rule skips every directory with that name anywhere in the

title: Fixing Path Exclusion Rules (187 to 743 Files Checked)
text: Repository. Data needed skipping in two places and keeping in two others. So, it splits a name list for things that are never source, and a prefix list for things excluded by where they sit. Deleting the entries alone made it 11 times slower, 6 seconds to 63, because it spawns one interpreter per file. A check nobody waits for stops being run, so the calls are batched. But batching has a trap. Windows command lines cap at 8,191 characters, not the 32,000 usually quoted. So, passed about 150 paths the spawn failed. The code fell back to one file at a time and the speed up disappeared while everything still passed. Chunks are kept well under the limit. Final result, four times the files and faster than before. Question three. Five things were broken on purpose to see whether the checker noticed. A syntax error appended to a step script caught and named. A truncated run envelope caught and named. title: Optimizing Execution Speed & Windows CLI Limits
text: Skipped tree still checked. and the deliberately broken JSON fixtures stayed invisible because those are supposed to be broken. Now, the part that matters. Episode 6's rule was to recount every figure from the file rather than trust the commit message. I did that here. 187 743 476 99 recipes. All four reproduce exactly. One does not. The message says the old run checked zero Python. It checked 39 one subsystem and mostly that subsystems own tests. No recipe step script which is the claim that actually matters but the headline number is wrong and it is my commit message. The second commit on the branch is the reason any of this can be evidence. title: Adversarial Audit: Deliberately Breaking 5 Elements
text: Hash of every script they ran, but Git was storing one line ending and checking out another. So a files hash changed with the machine. Line endings are now pinned repositorywide with shell scripts forced to the one ending that keeps a shebang readable. 2120 files normalized and 250 sampled at random. All 250 now hash identically to what is committed. Your turn. Open whatever check guards your project and make it print what it opened. Not whether it passed, but the count and the file types. Then compare that against what you believe it covers. The gap is the part nobody is checking. green because it wasn't looking.
